explain.say: In early 1944, at Bletchley Park in England, a room-sized machine called Colossus began reading the German high command's secret messages. Most of the codebreaking staff there were women, and Wrens operated the machines. Colossus was one of the first electronic digital computers. Look at the timeline from that machine to the phone in your pocket.

explain.say: How was the internet built? Watch the chain. In the 1960s Paul Baran and Donald Davies proposed packet switching, cutting data into small packets. In 1969 ARPANET linked American universities, in 1983 TCP/IP gave all networks one common language, and around 1991 Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in Geneva opened the World Wide Web to everyone. Which link do you use every day?

stages.label: The Web
stages.note: Pages and links, free for all, 1991.

stages.label: Mobile
stages.note: Phones put it in every pocket.

explain.say: Here are real numbers, approximately. About 1 percent of the world was online in 1995, about 29 percent in 2010 and about 67 percent in 2023. Meanwhile chips followed Moore's law, roughly doubling their transistors every two years: from 2,300 on Intel's first microprocessor in 1971 to billions today. Who are the third still offline?

Look at the map. The digital revolution has many homes: Silicon Valley's chip and software firms, CERN in Geneva, Bengaluru's IT services, Japanese electronics, and Nairobi, where the mobile money service M-Pesa, launched in 2007, let millions pay by text message without a bank. Why might a phone matter more than a bank branch?

Is it good for us? See both sides: knowledge, mobile money and new voices, but also surveillance, a digital divide and misinformation. Shoshana Zuboff warns of surveillance capitalism. Wonderful work. Challenge: write the history of one app you use, as a historian in 2100 might.

faq.q: When did the digital revolution begin?
faq.a: Historians often start with the electronic computers of the 1940s, such as Colossus at Bletchley Park in 1944 and ENIAC in 1945, then the transistor in 1947, the microchip and microprocessor, and the spread of personal computers, the internet and smartphones.

No single person. Paul Baran and Donald Davies developed packet switching, ARPANET first linked computers in 1969, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP, adopted in 1983, and Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web at CERN, opened to the public around 1991.

faq.q: Has the digital revolution been good for the world?
faq.a: It has spread knowledge, created new industries and services such as mobile money, and helped people organise. Critics point to surveillance, misinformation, a digital divide between and within countries, and the power of a few large platforms; Shoshana Zuboff calls this surveillance capitalism.

faq.q: How many people use the internet?
faq.a: Roughly 1 percent of the world's people were online in 1995, about 29 percent in 2010 and about 67 percent in 2023, by International Telecommunication Union estimates. About a third of humanity remains offline.

Gordon Moore's observation, from 1965 and revised in 1975, that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every two years. Intel's 4004 of 1971 had 2,300 transistors; leading chips today have billions.

facts: Colossus began breaking German Lorenz codes at Bletchley Park in 1944.
The first ARPANET message was sent in October 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989.

quiz.say: Moore's law says transistors double about every two years. Starting from 2,300 in 1971, about how many would there be in 1975?
